title: Praxis School Librarian (5312) - 200 Source Questions + 100 Independent Practice Questions + 200 Guided Review
description: Contains 200 original source questions, 100 assistant-authored independent practice questions, and 200 source-derived guided-review activities. The assistant audit found 143 distinct independent content kernels. Two 100-item diagnostics and a 120-item simulation with source-rich feedback and learning support for beginning school librarians.
contentReview: Assistant audit completed: 300 independent-practice items contain 143 distinct content kernels and 157 parallel variants under the normalized test. 200 additional activities are guided reasoning transformations, not independent exam questions. The 500-distinct-question target is not met.
simulationNote: The simulation matches the published 5312 question count, time, and five-domain distribution. It uses single-choice practice items; the official test may use several selected-response interaction types.
disclaimer: Independent preparation material, not affiliated with or endorsed by ETS, AASL, or ALA. Results are not official forms, scaled scores, pass predictions, licenses, legal advice, copyright determinations, privacy determinations, or substitutes for current state and local requirements.

domains.label: Information Access in the Learning Environment

items.prompt: A school librarian is reviewing needs assessment after noticing uneven learner outcomes. Which action is most defensible?
choices: Combine disaggregated use, achievement, curriculum, stakeholder, and access data before setting program priorities.
Use annual print circulation totals alone to determine every instructional and purchasing priority for the year.
Roll last year’s library improvement plan forward unchanged so program expectations stay steady for staff.
Survey frequent regular library visitors alone and generalize their preferences across the entire school.
items.rationale: A defensible needs assessment triangulates quantitative and qualitative evidence and looks for groups whose needs or access may be hidden by schoolwide averages.
choiceRationales: Correct. A defensible needs assessment triangulates quantitative and qualitative evidence and looks for groups whose needs or access may be hidden by schoolwide averages.
Circulation totals count checkouts yet miss database access, instructional collaboration, nonusers, and subgroup equity gaps across the school.
Repeating last year’s plan ignores shifts in enrollment, curriculum standards, student needs, and newly documented access barriers.
Sampling only frequent visitors introduces severe selection bias and omits the very students currently underserved by the library program.

items.prompt: A school librarian is reviewing mission and goals after noticing uneven learner outcomes. Which action is most defensible?
choices: Align the library mission and measurable goals with building priorities, student needs, open use, and freedom.
Draft annual library goals primarily around hardware and furniture purchases rather than student learning outcomes.
Adopt a generic model mission statement from an external handbook without gathering local stakeholder input.
Operate the library program independently from classroom curriculum priorities and building improvement plans.
items.rationale: Program goals should connect library services to learning while preserving the school librarian’s professional responsibilities and the rights of all learners.
choiceRationales: Correct. Program goals should connect library services to learning while preserving the school librarian’s professional responsibilities and the rights of all learners.
Equipment purchases are inputs rather than student outcomes; goals should show how resources expand equitable learning and inquiry.
A generic statement drafted without local input lacks ownership and fails to reflect the community’s distinct learner needs.
Separating the library from schoolwide curriculum weakens collaboration, instructional relevance, and measurable impact on student achievement across grades.

items.prompt: A school librarian is reviewing budget stewardship after noticing uneven learner outcomes. Which action is most defensible?
choices: Build a transparent, data-driven fiscal plan tying spending to priorities, lifecycle costs, access, and equity.
Spend remaining year-end funds rapidly on the newest commercial gadgets regardless of documented student needs.
Divide collection funds evenly across every format without reviewing usage patterns, curriculum gaps, or access.
List initial purchase prices alone while omitting annual licensing renewals, upkeep, accessibility, and replacement.
items.rationale: Sound budgeting considers total cost of ownership, documented needs, instructional value, accessibility, and whether resources expand equitable opportunity.
choiceRationales: Correct. Sound budgeting considers total cost of ownership, documented needs, instructional value, accessibility, and whether resources expand equitable opportunity.
Buying unaligned products wastes scarce public funds and leaves documented curriculum, language, and accessibility priorities underfunded.
Equal format splits ignore sharply differing curricular needs, digital access realities, and subgroup demand across the building.
Omitting renewal, maintenance, and replacement costs creates multi-year budget cliffs that threaten sustained access to vital resources.

items.prompt: A school librarian is reviewing program evaluation after noticing uneven learner outcomes. Which action is most defensible?
choices: Use process, participation, availability, and achievement data to evaluate delivery and refine operations.
Report total annual book checkouts alone as comprehensive evidence of the school library’s instructional impact.
Alter staffing, scheduling, and instruction at once without documenting how planned changes were implemented.
Claim strong schoolwide academic impact strictly from informal positive hallway comments shared by visitors.
items.rationale: Evaluation is strongest when measures match stated goals, implementation is documented, evidence is disaggregated, and findings lead to a monitored improvement cycle.
choiceRationales: Correct. Evaluation is strongest when measures match stated goals, implementation is documented, evidence is disaggregated, and findings lead to a monitored improvement cycle.
Checkout totals track circulation volume yet fail to capture inquiry learning, co-teaching outcomes, or equitable subgroup access.
Changing multiple undocumented variables at once prevents the librarian from identifying what worked or diagnosing implementation gaps.
Informal hallway praise reflects selective personal impressions rather than systematic participation, equitable access, and student-outcome evaluation data.

items.prompt: A school librarian is reviewing policy and operations after noticing uneven learner outcomes. Which action is most defensible?
choices: Set clear, consistent procedures with stakeholder input, law, safety, privacy, reconsideration, and appeals.
Handle each collection or access dispute informally case by case without relying on written policy criteria.
Apply looser approval or access standards to popular viewpoints while scrutinizing unfamiliar topics more strictly.
Promise absolute secrecy over every student library conversation regardless of safety or mandated-reporting law.
items.rationale: Written, viewpoint-neutral procedures protect access and due process while helping staff respond consistently and consult authorized decision makers when facts are complex.
choiceRationales: Correct. Written, viewpoint-neutral procedures protect access and due process while helping staff respond consistently and consult authorized decision makers when facts are complex.
Informal ad-hoc handling invites inconsistency, bias, and legal vulnerability when written board-approved procedures should govern fairly.
Viewpoint-based double standards violate core intellectual freedom principles and leave collection governance open to serious legal and community challenge.
Student privacy is vital, yet librarians cannot promise secrecy that overrides immediate safety or statutory reporting obligations.

items.prompt: A school librarian is reviewing collection development after noticing uneven learner outcomes. Which action is most defensible?
choices: Apply board selection policy, curriculum and community data, professional reviews, diversity audits, and access.
Select new collection titles primarily from genres and authors the school librarian personally enjoys reading.
Use bestseller popularity charts as the single deciding criterion for building every section of the collection.
Avoid acquiring resources representing unfamiliar cultural or intellectual perspectives to prevent potential complaints.
items.rationale: Collection decisions should follow documented criteria and build a relevant, representative, accessible collection rather than reflecting one person’s preferences.
choiceRationales: Correct. Collection decisions should follow documented criteria and build a relevant, representative, accessible collection rather than reflecting one person’s preferences.
Personal reading taste narrows collection breadth and overlooks diverse learner identities, grade-level curriculum standards, and vital accessibility formats.
Popularity matters for engagement, yet relying on it alone neglects curricular depth, authoritative nonfiction, and underrepresented voices.
Self-censorship to avoid controversy violates intellectual freedom and deprives learners of windows, mirrors, and balanced inquiry.

items.prompt: A school librarian is reviewing cataloging and metadata after noticing uneven learner outcomes. Which action is most defensible?
choices: Apply consistent descriptive and subject fields, authorized entry points, and unbiased local notes.
Create a custom informal classification rule for each new book so shelving reflects intuitive daily judgments.
Strip subject headings out of catalog records to shorten cataloging time and simplify search displays.
Keep outdated stigmatizing subject labels in local records even when neutral current terminology is available.
items.rationale: Consistent, inclusive metadata supports discovery, interoperability, and user independence; local practice should be documented and reviewed for harmful or obsolete language.
choiceRationales: Correct. Consistent, inclusive metadata supports discovery, interoperability, and user independence; local practice should be documented and reviewed for harmful or obsolete language.
Inconsistent ad-hoc rules break collocation and make it difficult for students and educators to locate related resources reliably.
Removing subject headings severely limits topical discovery when students search by concept rather than exact title or author.
Outdated biased subject labels alienate student learners and impede accurate topical discovery when respectful standardized terms already exist.

items.prompt: A school librarian is reviewing weeding and retention after noticing uneven learner outcomes. Which action is most defensible?
choices: Apply written weeding criteria covering accuracy, condition, relevance, use, duplication, and curriculum.
Discard every book that did not circulate during the past academic year without checking curricular value.
Keep scientifically outdated or inaccurate reference volumes on shelves so library stacks continue looking full.
Pull challenged viewpoints from shelves quietly during routine weeding without using formal reconsideration policy.
items.rationale: Weeding is a planned collection-development function, not censorship; multiple criteria and exceptions for enduring, local, and curricular value are essential.
choiceRationales: Correct. Weeding is a planned collection-development function, not censorship; multiple criteria and exceptions for enduring, local, and curricular value are essential.
Low annual checkout can reflect poor display or shifting units rather than low value; weeding requires multi-factor criteria.
Retaining inaccurate or misleading materials harms student inquiry and clutters shelves so quality current titles are harder to find.
Using routine weeding as stealth censorship circumvents transparent, viewpoint-neutral board reconsideration procedures and fair due process protections.
